in accordance with its functional meaning, it is discussed as being both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted.
What is the meaning of this?
For those such as the candidate for the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin),
the fact that they follow noble wisdom to sever the fetters is designated as "correct."
The conventional knowledge that abandons the fetters is explained as being "conformable";
this is precisely the untainted (anāsrava),
whereas "conformability" itself is tainted (sāsrava).
Question: Is it the case that all possess both types, or are there those who do not?
Explanation: [It is said:]...
[The interlocutor] prepares the requisites and asks:
"If there are those who sever the afflictions (kleśa) using exclusively the Noble Path, how can there still be 'concomitance' (anvaya)?"
If there is someone who uses only conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*) to sever the fetters, how can this be correct?
It is because they are mutually established through shared practice.
How are they mutually established?
When one uses the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) to sever the afflictions of the lower stages,
one immediately accomplishes the tainted merits (*sāsrava-guṇa*) of the higher stages.
If one uses conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) to sever the afflictions of the lower stages, [the same result follows].
It also accomplishes the untainted virtues of the higher stages;
thus, they are equally complete.
The fruit of arhatship is exclusively untainted.

Question: Regarding the fruits of *sakṛdāgāmin* and *anāgāmin*, according to the Abhidharma, both explain that conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) serves as the "concordant fruit" (*anuvartaka-phala*).
This concordant fruit is explained as being with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Why is it that the fruit of arhatship alone is specifically termed "untainted" (anāsrava)?
The explanation states that conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) serves as its accompanying fruit.

Because there is no capacity whatsoever to counteract the fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), there is no "consequent fruit" (*anvaya-phala*).
Because there is no consequent fruit, it is purely designated as "untainted" (*anāsrava*).
Such is the distinction between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted; this concludes the two gateways.
Next, there is the distinction between the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Morality, concentration, wisdom, and so forth are conditioned;
the merit of analytical cessation is unconditioned.
If these two are distinguished according to the paths of cessation and cultivation, all conditioned merits are termed "approaches" (mārga),
while unconditioned merits are collectively judged as "fruits" (phala). If,
however, they are distinguished according to the four approaches and four fruits:
Within the preceding [causes], there are both conditioned and unconditioned [phenomena];
it is likewise within the fruits. Question:
Since both types are present within the aforementioned [category],
one must distinguish which of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are correct and which are not.
There are two interpretations regarding this.
Regarding the distinction between the two types—

conditioned and unconditioned— within the same category of discernment, there is a correct principle for each of the two fruits (conditioned and unconditioned) when viewed in relation to the two paths (conditioned and unconditioned).
What are their characteristics?
Because the aspiration for conditioned phenomena and the conditioned fruits arise from their mutual production of similar types, they are termed "correct.
Furthermore, upon reaching the fruit, one attains the conditioned merits that were present within those causes.
Because they collectively accomplish a single fruit, they are also termed "correct.
Within the stage of "convergence," the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is called "correct" because it forms a homogeneous category in relation to the unconditioned fruit.
Furthermore, upon reaching the fruit, one attains those unconditioned merits that were present within the cause.
Because they collectively produce a single fruit, they are also termed "correct.
Second, the distinction between strength and weakness:
among the causes, there are those that act in concert toward the same fruit.
That which possesses power is judged as "directly heading toward" (abhimukha);
that which is unconditioned and lacks power is judged as "following toward" (anugata).
What is the meaning of this?
Because the power of cultivation regarding conditioned phenomena within the cause can produce conditioned meritorious qualities within the fruit,
it is called "correct.
Furthermore, it can sever the fetters and lead toward the unconditioned meritorious qualities within the fruit.
Therefore, by looking toward those virtues, they may also be called "correct.

As for the virtues of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they are called "conforming" when in the stage of application (*prayoga*), because they lack the capacity of the former two; thus, they are not called "correct."
Question: Among the two kinds of qualities within the fruit—conditioned and unconditioned—which is the actual fruit?
There are also two interpretations for this.
When members of the same category are compared, both are considered "correct fruits" (*samyak-phala*).
Among these fruits, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is called a "correct fruit" because it arises from the conditioned practice of the path of approach (*prayoga-mārga*).
Furthermore, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) within the fruit is also termed "correct," as it is correctly subsumed by the unconditioned virtues achieved within the cause.
The second [classification] is made in relation to the mind that seeks [the result]:
the unconditioned is the primary fruit,
while the conditioned is the concordant fruit.
Why is this so? Because the sages fundamentally cultivate the path for the sake of nirvāṇa;
the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is precisely that which the worthy and noble seek.
Therefore, these are the true fruits.
Because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are objects of aversion, they are not true fruits.
This is precisely because conditioned phenomena are what one must weary of and abandon, and thus are not true fruits.
Once the afflictions have been exhausted, even the Path is relinquished;
it is the unconditioned that is sought after,
for it is the true fruit.
Ultimately seeking realization.
Such is the conclusion of these three gates concerning the distinction between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Next, their characteristics will be distinguished according to the stages of dhyāna.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, when the derivative states are subsumed under their primary bases, there are nine dhyāna stages,
namely the eight dhyānas plus the lightning-like samādhi within the desire realm.
When the derivative states are distinguished from their primary bases, there are ten dhyāna stages.
Within the first dhyāna, the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*) is distinguished separately; including those that extend to the others, ten stages are taught.
If one follows the Abhidharma, by subsuming the branches under the root, there are eight dhyāna levels, namely the so-called eight dhyānas.
Since that school does not assert the existence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the desire realm, there are only eight [stages].
When the subsidiary stages are distinguished from the fundamental dhyāna grounds, there are ten;
within the first dhyāna, the preliminary stage (*anāgamyam*) and the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntaram*) are separately distinguished and added to the others to make ten.
The stages of dhyāna are likewise.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, the four paths and four fruits all rely on the stages from the first dhyāna up to nothingness (*ākiṃcanya*).
Because these seven locations serve as the basis for the untainted (*anāsrava*), they are called the "seven meditative bases" (*saptaniśrayasamādhi*).
Furthermore, based on the desire realm, one eliminates the non-perceptual stage by means of the lightning-like samādhi.
A question is asked:
The Abhidharma proclaims that the spheres of emptiness, consciousness, and nothingness do not give rise to insight.
Why does the *Tattvasiddhi* teach that the first fruit (*phala*) and the first candidate (*pratipannaka*) both rely on the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
Their schools differ and their established tenets vary.
According to the *Abhidharma*, the formless realm does not take the contaminated seeds of the lower realms as its object for the contemplation of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*).
Nor does one take the lower contaminated states (*sāsrava*) as the object of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) for the contemplation of cessation and the path.
Therefore, the formless realm (*ārūpya*) does not give rise to insight (*darśana*).
However, since the *Satyasiddhi* establishes that [the formless] can serve as an object, insight is also produced based on the formless realm.
He asked again:
"Why does the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception not serve as a basis?
Because it lacks the untainted (anāsrava) state."
Question: The *Tattvasiddhi* proclaims that one enters the attainment of cessation after a non-perceptual, untainted mind.
Why is it said that there is no untainted (anāsrava) state in the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana)?
The explanation is:
in the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there exists only the untainted state of conforming to the habitual meditative observation (pūrvābhyāsa-vipaśyanā).
There is no untainted (*anāsrava*) severance of fetters through the cultivation of increase-contemplation (*vṛddhānupaśyanā*).

For this reason, one does not rely on anything else; rather, one follows the previous practice of contemplation and first employs the lower meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) to give rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*).

One contemplates the suffering, impermanence, and so forth of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Thereafter, one uses that mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to take as its object the suffering, impermanence, and so forth previously contemplated;
this is called "anuloma-ānupūrvaka-vihāra-darśana" (sequential contemplation in accordance with the previous [stages], which is untainted).
Because this mind is subtle and its power of investigation is weak,
it does not give rise to the increase of insight (bhāvanā) or the outflow-free state (anāsrava).

According to the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā), the two fruits of srotāpanna and sakṛdāgāmin, as well as their respective paths of approach (pratipannaka), exist only in the future dhyāna and do not extend to other stages.
It is precisely because these [beings] have not yet exhausted their fetters of desire and have not attained the higher dhyānas that they do not rely [upon them].
The candidate for the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmipratipannaka) is comprised within either six stages:
the four fundamental dhyānas, the preliminary stage (anāgamya), and the intermediate stage (dhyānāntara).
Furthermore, such a person following the sequential path necessarily relies upon the preliminary stage.
That person of sequential practice has not yet exhausted the fetters of desire and has not yet attained the remaining dhyānas;
for this reason, they do not rely [on them].
A person who has transcended may rely on the *anāgamya* stage up to the fourth dhyāna.
If they enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) by relying on the *anāgamya* stage, it is subsumed under the *anāgamya*;
likewise, if they enter the path of seeing by relying on the fourth dhyāna, it is subsumed under the fourth dhyāna.
In that school, the four formless attainments do not enter the path of seeing;
for this reason, they are not relied upon.
The fruit of *anāgāmin* is likewise subsumed within the six stages.
This is similar to what was stated previously.
Those who follow in succession are likewise included within the category of those yet to come. Why is this so?

That person of successive practice uses the untainted [attainment] produced by future dhyāna as the path of non-obstruction to sever the fetters of the desire realm until they are exhausted; having done so,
they again use the untainted [attainment] produced by that same dhyāna as the path of liberation.
Therefore, it is subsumed under the future [state].
One does not use the untainted [attainment] produced by other dhyānas to sever the fetters of the desire realm.
For this reason, this fruit does not reside in other seeds.
Those who have transcended are either included in the future [birth] or up to the fourth dhyāna; the meaning is the same as explained previously.
Those who are candidates for arhatship (arhattvaphalapratipannaka) are included in nine stages.
The fundamental four dhyānas, the preliminary (anāgāmya), the intermediate (dhyānāntara), and the three formless attainments—
these are comprised within ten stages when the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) is added.
The untainted (anāsrava) right direction is subsumed under nine stages (bhūmi).
If one speaks of it as including the tainted (sāsrava) according to its various directions, then it is subsumed under ten stages.
How is it that the untainted is subsumed under nine stages?
The untainted [dharmas] are of two kinds:
first, those that arise manifest through cultivation by application while focusing on their objects;
second, those that are merely accomplished through cultivation by acquisition.
Regarding the practice of cultivation within the nine stages, whether these [factors] are present or absent is not fixed;
they may be present in one, two, three, four, five, six, or even up to nine kinds.
What is the meaning of this?

If there is someone who uses exclusively the outflow-free (anāsrava) states generated within the future dhyāna (*anāgāmya-dhyāna*) to sever the fetters of the first dhyāna up to those of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), this is subsumed under a single stage.
The same principle applies whether one uses the first dhyāna or the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).

Alternatively, if there is a person who uses the outflow-free [wisdom] produced by the stage of future dhyāna and the first dhyāna to sever the fetters of the upper realms and advance toward arhatship, then it is subsumed under two stages.
Alternatively, by employing the untainted [wisdom] produced in the intermediate stage of the future first dhyāna,
one severs the fetters of the upper realms, which are then comprised within three stages.
Alternatively, by employing the untainted [wisdom] produced in the first three [stages] plus that produced in the second dhyāna.
The severing of the fetters of the upper realms is subsumed under four stages;
alternatively, if the first four are employed along with the third dhyāna, it is subsumed under five stages;
if the fourth dhyāna is added, it is subsumed under six stages.
If the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana) is added, it is subsumed within the seven stages.
If the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana) is added, it is subsumed within the eight dhyānas.
If the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) is added, it is subsumed within the nine stages.
Within these stages, all untainted [paths] function such that the lower [levels] sever the higher,
but the higher do not sever the lower;
the practice of cultivation is thus.
If one discusses the cultivation through attainment (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), all [stages] are fully endowed with the untainted states (*anāsrava*) of the nine stages.
How are they fully endowed?
There are four meanings of "endowment."
When pure [factors] are compared with one another, the lower serves as the basis for attaining the higher.
When an Anāgāmin uses the pure factors of the lower stage to sever the fetters of the lower stage,
he simultaneously attains the pure merits of the higher stages.

Just as when one uses the untainted [attainment] arising from the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*) or the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*) of the first dhyāna to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the first dhyāna, one then attains the untainted merit of the second dhyāna;
so it is in all such cases.
Regarding the mutual relationship between the two types of untainted [attainments], one may obtain a lower stage by relying on a higher stage.
There are those who, while still ordinary beings, attain anything from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
subsequently, having become noble ones, they employ whichever stage is appropriate to give rise to untainted states that sever the fetters of the higher realms.
At that time, one attains the untainted (*anāsrava*) merits of the lower stage.
Thirdly, regarding the tainted (*sāsrava*) in relation to the untainted, by relying on the lower, one accomplishes the higher.

For example, when employing the preparatory wisdom (*prāyogika-jñāna*) of the second dhyāna to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the first dhyāna, one then attains the untainted merits of the second dhyāna.
All such cases are like this:
when one relies on the higher [stages] to attain the lower with respect to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) from the perspective of the outflowing (*sāsrava*),
it is as when employing the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the second dhyāna.
By severing the fetters of the first dhyāna, one attains the untainted (anāsrava) merits of the first dhyāna.
This is because they share the same counteractive cultivation (pratipakṣa-bhāvanā). What is meant by "sharing the same counteractive cultivation"?
The untainted (anāsrava) first dhyāna can also counteract the afflictions of the first dhyāna up to all afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, the conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) belonging to the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) of the second dhyāna level can also counteract the afflictions of the first dhyāna.
It is called "common remedy.

Even the conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the preparatory stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-prayoga*) can serve as a remedy for the fetters of nothingness;
it is therefore called a "common remedy."
Because they are of the same nature, when one employs the skillful means and conventional knowledge of the second dhyāna to sever the afflictions of the first dhyāna,
one immediately attains the untainted merit of the first dhyāna.
Although one may attain it, it is only a small portion and not much;
one merely attains a single part of the outflow-free state that serves as an antidote to the fetters of the first dhyāna,
while all else remains unattained.
Therefore, it is called a "minor portion.
How is it attained? It is at the time when that path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) effects complete abandonment.
One should sever this fetter that arises at the limit of the attainment of the untainted mind;

even when employing the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) belonging to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) to sever the afflictions of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
They also attain the untainted merit of the first dhyāna;
yet though they attain it, it is slight and not much.
They merely attain a portion of the untainted [state] that severs one part of the fetters associated with nothingness (*ākiṃcanya*).
None of the others are obtained;
therefore, it is said that they are not many.

This is because, when the skillful means and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) of those various stages are compared with the untainted merit (*anāsrava-guṇa*) of the stage of the first dhyāna, such is the case for their attainment.
One should expect that among the remaining stages, those untainted (*anāsrava*) merits which are to be counteracted by the same [antidote] will be acquired equally;
however, those which are not to be counteracted by the same [antidote] will not be acquired at all.
The stages subsumed under the candidate for Arhatship (*arhattvaphalapratipannaka*) are likewise.
The fruit of arhatship is also comprised within nine stages:
the four fundamental dhyānas, the preliminary stage (anāgāmya), the intermediate stage (dhyānāntara), and the three formless attainments.
The untainted (anāsrava) states of these nine stages are all capable of counteracting the fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, whereby one attains arhatship.
Therefore, within this context, if distinguished according to their cultivation through practice, they may be subsumed under the future [realm],
up to and including being subsumed under nothingness (*ākiṃcanya*).
When one uses future dhyāna to sever the fetters and realize the fruit, it is then subsumed under the future.
The same applies to the other stages.
If one considers them according to their attainment through cultivation, they are all subsumed within the nine stages;
for when one attains Arhatship, one simultaneously acquires all the untainted (anāsrava) qualities of those nine stages as their fruit.
The four gates of the stages of dhyāna are thus concluded.
Next, the meaning of "transcending" and "not transcending" will be examined;
as the schools differ, their explanations vary accordingly.
In the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), among all noble ones (*ārya*), there are none who transcend [the stages].
Since that school maintains that ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) do not sever their fetters (*saṃyojana*),
in the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā) system, there are no "leapers" (*atikrāntaka*) among the four candidates for the fruits (*pratipannaka*).
Among the four fruits, the fruit of *srotāpanna* likewise admits no transcendence;
only the fruits of *sakṛdāgāmin* and *anāgāmin* involve both transcendence and non-transcendence.
According to that school, because ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) can sever the fetters, it is said that there is the possibility of transcendence.
What are the characteristics? There is a person who, while still an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), has not yet severed any fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Upon entering the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), they reach the sixteenth moment, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
One is merely named a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer).
Alternatively, there may be someone who, while still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), has already severed from one to five grades of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm.
Subsequently, upon entering the Path of Seeing and reaching the sixteenth moment, the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna),
this is likewise included within the stage of the Srotāpanna fruit;
however, one cannot yet be designated as a candidate for the Sakṛdāgāmin fruit.
Because there is no transcendent realization within the path of application (prayoga-mārga),

or alternatively, when a person who has previously severed the fetters of desire up to the sixth category enters the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) and reaches the sixteenth moment, the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna).
He does not become a srotāpanna, nor does he become one progressing toward the stage of sakṛdāgāmin;
rather, he transcends these to directly realize the second fruit,
that of sakṛdāgāmin, because all the afflictions to be abandoned by a sakṛdāgāmin have already been eliminated.
Alternatively, there may be a person who first severs the fetters of desire up to the exhaustion of the eighth grade,
and subsequently enters the path of seeing; at the time of the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) of the sixteenth moment of the path,
they likewise transcend [the stages] and are subsumed under the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin.
Yet they cannot be called "candidates for the fruit of non-returning" (anāgāmipratipannaka),
because within the stage of candidacy there is no realization by way of skipping stages.
Alternatively, there may be someone who has previously severed the fetters of desire up to the exhaustion of the ninth grade.
Later, upon entering the Path of Seeing and reaching the sixteenth moment, the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna),
one does not become a *srotāpanna* who leaps over to realize the third fruit, that of the *anāgāmin*.
This is because all the afflictions to be abandoned by a person on the stage of *anāgāmin* have already been eliminated.
Alternatively, there may be someone who first abandons all afflictions from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness,
and subsequently enters the path of seeing until reaching the sixteenth moment, the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna).
This is also subsumed under the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) by way of transcendence;
however, it cannot be termed the "candidate for arhatship" (arhattvapratipannaka),
because there is no realization by transcendence within the stage of candidacy.
Question: For what reason is there a leap (*vyutkrānta*) within the fruition (*phala*), but no leap within the intermediate state (*antara*)?
The explanation says:
The transcendental realization must necessarily occur within the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*).
That sixteenth moment of the path of application, the knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), is the point where one realizes the fruit of cessation.
It is at this stage that the six grades of the fetters of desire and the nine grades [of the higher realms] have been previously severed and brought to their end.
It is also the place where one attains the fruit through cessation;
because its meaning accords with this, one attains transcendence and realization.
All other categories, being situated in this place of cessation and realization, do not accord [with it].
Therefore, there is no "leaping" realization.
This is because among all these stages of progress (*pratipannaka*), there is no leaping.
[The opponent] asks:
If the path of comparison (mārga-sādṛśya) accords with the meaning of the fruit at the limit of those six or nine grades and one is able to attain transcendental realization (vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti),
why is it that the preceding fifteen moments of mind, which accord with the preparatory stage (prayoga-mārga),
cannot likewise attain transcendental realization of that preparatory stage?
The commentary states:

During the preceding fifteen moments of mind, the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the single stage of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) have not yet been exhausted;
those to be abandoned through the sequential path (*anupūrva-prahāṇa*) remain未尽 (*ajīrṇa*, not yet fully eliminated).
How could one transcend and realize [the fruit]?
Therefore, transcendental realization occurs exclusively within the path and subsequent knowledges (mārga-anvaya-jñāna), and not in other minds.
This is truly because there is no transcendental realization within the preceding fifteen moments of mind.
In all directions, there is nothing that transcends this.
It is asked:
At the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one first severs the six grades and then exhausts the nine grades of afflictions.
Why was he not immediately named a Sakṛdāgāmin or an Anāgāmin at that time?
It was only when he reached the stage of the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) on the Path that he received those names.
To explain:
Those who have attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin and Anāgāmin must necessarily be free from the delusions of view.
Although they may have severed six grades or even all nine grades of delusions during their time as ordinary beings,
because the delusions of view still persist, they cannot be designated as Sakṛdāgāmins or Anāgāmins.

At the time of the knowledge of conformity to the Path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), the afflictions of the realm of vision (*darśana-heya*) are finally exhausted; therefore, it is only at this stage that it receives its name. Question:
Why is there no "leap-over" [attainment] regarding the first fruit?
Because nothing can be attained prior to the first fruit.
Furthermore, an ordinary person cannot completely sever the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) associated with the views.
Therefore, there is no "leap-over" [attainment].
Why is there no leap-over for the fruit of Arhatship?
It is because ordinary beings cannot completely sever all the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Having thus concluded the discussion on whether there is anyone who transcends these five gates,
the text next clarifies the meaning of falling back and not falling back.
Within the stage of the Srotāpanna-pratipannaka (the candidate for stream-entry), there is both falling back and no falling back.
What is the meaning of this?
The five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-vastu-sthāpana*) and the general and specific applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are invariably subject to regression.
The two stages of "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) may be either regressive or non-regressive.
What is the meaning of this?
According to the Abhidharma, from the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) upward, there is no longer the possibility of severing the roots of goodness to become an icchantika;
this is what is called "non-retrogression."
If one allows other transgressions to arise and falls into the three evil realms,
this is termed "retrogression. However,
if one relies on *nirvāṇa*, the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes will never arise again.
Furthermore, when one severs the roots of goodness and becomes an icchantika,
this is called "non-retrogression. Yet,
upon encountering evil associates, one may give rise to the ten unwholesome actions and fall into the three evil realms.
This is termed "retrogression.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, one will furthermore not again commit the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes, nor sever the roots of goodness;
nor will one again commit the ten evil deeds—whether major or minor—to fall into the three evil realms.
This is called "non-retrogression.

Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi* states that the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), and so forth constitute "superior right view," whereby one does not fall into the evil realms for hundreds of thousands of lifetimes throughout successive births and deaths.
When one gives rise to afflictions and performs light karma, resulting in the cycle of rebirth among humans and devas,
this is called "retrogression. However,
the stages of patience (*kṣānti*), the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), and the mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are invariably non-retrogressive.
There is likewise no possibility of falling back from the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
Regarding the stages of the candidate for *sakṛdāgāmin*, the candidate for *anāgāmin*, and the candidate for *arhat*,
according to the *Tattvasiddhi*, all the noble qualities possessed within these stages are entirely non-retrogressive.
If there is regression, it is merely a regression from meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
According to the Abhidharma (*Vibhāṣā*), all noble qualities (*ārya-guṇa*) possessed within this stage are also lost.
What is the meaning of "non-regression"?
There are four types of distinctions.
First, the distinction according to faculties:
those with dull faculties undergo regression.
Those of sharp faculties do not fall back,
because those who are immovable by nature are certain not to fall back.
Second, there is a distinction based on cultivation.
Those who are negligent and lax will regress;
those who practice with single-minded devotion will not regress.
This is the third classification based on conduct.
Those who sever the fetters by employing a mixture of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) may still experience regression;
those who sever the fetters by employing exclusively the untainted (*anāsrava*) are firm and do not regress.
Fourth, the classification according to the realms of existence (*gati*).
There is falling away among humans,
because there are many causes and conditions for falling away among humans;
in the heavens, however, there is no falling away.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"The gods do not fall back.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, the fruit of arhatship is invariably non-retrogressive.
If there is regression, it is only a regression from meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
According to the Abhidharma as well, there is both regression and non-regression;
what is the meaning of this?
There are six types of discrimination.
The first is discrimination based on the afflictions (*kleśa*).
There are two kinds of afflictions.
First, the afflictions that lead to rebirth,
which give rise to false craving and so forth at the time of taking birth;
second, the afflictions that obstruct the Path.
When greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth arise in dependence on conditions, they obstruct the Noble Path.
In such cases, it is said that an Arhat "recedes" when these afflictions that obstruct the path are permitted to arise even for a moment.
The ultimate non-arising of afflictions upon rebirth is called "non-retrogression.
Second, there is the analysis according to the causes and conditions of afflictions.
There are two kinds of causes and conditions:
the internal and the external.
Afflictions arise from the unabated nature of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and from improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
That which is called "internal" gives rise to fetters; that which is designated as "external" consists of the five sense objects.
That Arhat has already severed internal causes;
because there are no internal causes from which afflictions arise, he is called "non-retrogressive.
However, it is possible for afflictions to arise due to external conditions.
This is called "retrogression.
It refers to the temporary arising of sensual defilement upon observing an object of intense craving that has become predominant;
because one subsequently severs it, it is called "transcending birth."
Third, distinguishing by way of the faculties:
those with dull faculties undergo regression,
while those with sharp faculties do not.
What is the meaning of this?

Those Arhats possess six types of spiritual natures: those subject to regression, those who attain through reflection, those who guard their attainment, those who abide in their state, those who advance, and those who are immovable.
The meaning is as explained later:
those of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) are invariably subject to falling away,
while those of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*) are invariably not subject to falling away.
The meanings of "contemplation," "protection," "abiding," and "progress" are not fixed.
If a person subject to regression practices for progress, they may still regress;
however, if a person not subject to regression practices for progress, there is only abiding and only progress—there is no possibility of regression.
Fourth, the distinction based on cultivation:
those who cultivate with single-minded dedication do not regress;
those who are distracted and lax do regress.
Therefore, it is stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* that there are five types of regression:
first, delighting in many affairs;
second, delighting in speaking of worldly matters.
Third, delighting in sleep;
fourth, delighting in associating with householders;
fifth, delighting in wandering about excessively.
These five matters cause a bhikṣu to fall back.
There are five distinctions regarding practice:
one who has become an achiever through dull faculties and the severance of fetters by means of the untainted (anāsrava) is never subject to falling back.
One who has severed the fetters by means of the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and so forth may still be subject to regression;
what is the meaning of this?
It is that such a person, by means of that conventional knowledge, grasps at the higher [realms].
Through the practice of revulsion toward the lower realms, one severs the fetters of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness; however,
the single stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is not treated by conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*),
but is severed by means of the untainted (*anāsrava*) path.
Because it is not fundamentally firm,
there is regression; therefore,
the analogy of the old man at the sand well is used.
It is like a sand well: although it may be lined with layers of bricks, it cannot avoid sinking and collapsing.
This case is likewise.
The sixth [point] is a classification according to realms (*dhātu*) and destinies (*gati*).
"Realms" refers to the three realms.
There is falling back in the desire realm,
whereas it does not exist in the higher realms.
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"If it is said that one will fall back, one will necessarily fall back;
even if it is said that one will surely advance, one will certainly advance."
It should be understood that this refers to Arhats of the desire realm,
not those of the two higher realms.
The desire realm possesses the causes and conditions for retrogression,
whereas the higher realms do not.
"Destinies" refers to the five destinies.
Among humans, Arhats may undergo regression;
among devas, there is no regression.
This is because among humans, there are many causes and conditions for regression.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"The various devas do not regress.
This is a rough explanation of the four stages of approach and the four fruits of realization.
Alternatively, they may be divided into thirteen,
as explained in the Abhidharma:
the seven persons of the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are counted as seven.
The path of seeing (darśanamārga) is divided into two types:
namely, the follower by faith (śraddhānusārin) and the follower by dharma (dharmānusārin).
A person of dull faculties who enters the path of seeing is called a follower by faith.
Because one initiates practice by trusting the words of the Noble Ones,
those of sharp faculties who enter the path of seeing the truths are called "Dharma-practitioners" (dharmānusārin),
for they initiate practice through seeing the Dharma with their own minds.
Including the preceding, there are nine.
Within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there are two types:
namely, those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
A person of dull faculties on the path of cultivation is called "liberated through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*),
because they attain liberation by trusting the words of the noble ones.
A person of sharp faculties on the path of cultivation is called "one who has attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
Because one attains liberation by seeing phenomena through one's own mind,
these two types are practiced throughout the preceding eleven stages, as well as within the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
This refers to those liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) and those not liberated by occasion (*asamayavimukta*).
A person of dull faculties who has attained the fruit of arhatship is called "liberated by occasion," because one of dull faculties attains liberation by depending on specific time and place.
Those of sharp faculties who have reached the fruit are called "liberated at any time" (asamayavimukta),
because those of sharp faculties do not need to wait for specific conditions to attain liberation.
Including the previous thirteen [types], there are [thus] fourteen.
Because there are six types of persons distinguished on the path of vision (*darśanamārga*),
the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"In terms of substance, it is said that there are six."
Alternatively, they may be divided into fourteen,
as explained in the Abhidharma.
Prior to the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga), the seven preliminary aids (saptaprayoga) are taught.

In the path of seeing (darśanamārga), there are those who practice through faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who practice through the Dharma (dharmānusārin). In the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), there are those liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
Including the former [two], these constitute eleven types.

Among those who have attained the state of non-returner (anāgāmin), one who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is called "one realized through the body" (kāyasākṣin); including the previous twelve types, there are thirteen.
Within the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), there are said to be those liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta) and those liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta).
Including the previous ones, there are fourteen.
One who has not attained the attainment of cessation is called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñā-vimukta).
One who has attained the attainment of cessation is called "doubly liberated" (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta).
It can also be divided into fifteen:

Second is "transmigrating to another life" (upapadya-parinirvāyin).

Within the higher realms, they do not attain parinirvāṇa in their first body,

Among those nine who are liberated through faith, there are individuals with dull faculties.

Eleventh are the bodily witnesses (*kāyasākṣin*):

The details are as explained later.
Within the category of arhats, there are nine distinctions;
when combined with the preceding categories, they constitute twenty-seven types of persons in total.
First is the sign of regression.
This person is the most dull-witted;
because of their dull faculties, they will inevitably regress from the concentration they have attained.
The second is guarding the signs.
With fewer faculties than before,
one guards oneself deeply, and it is possible not to fall back.
Third is the sign of death:
the faculties become even more acute than before,
yet one feels a profound aversion toward all states of existence and is unable to attain meditative concentration.
Having obtained it, one fears losing it;
thus seeking to take one's own life is called the sign of death.
Fourth is the characteristic of abiding:
the samādhi attained neither regresses nor advances.
Fifth is the characteristic of being capable of advancing.
The samādhis attained become increasingly superior and enhanced.
Regarding the six indestructible characteristics:
the various causes and conditions cannot destroy the samādhis attained.
Seventh is the mark of non-retrogression;
the supreme person’s attained merits are entirely without retrogression.
Eighth is liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).
Among the aforementioned persons, those who do not attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) are called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñāvimukta);

Each of these will be explained in detail later as they are established in the *Tattvasiddhi*.
Furthermore, there is another group of twenty-seven persons.
As stated in the *Madhyama Āgama*, "Chapter on the Field of Merit" (*Puṇyakṣetra-varga*),

without extending to those prior to such realization.
What are its characteristics?
There was a householder there named Anāthapiṇḍada.
"I ask the Tathāgata:
how many kinds of persons who are fields of merit exist in the world?
The Buddha replied, "There are two."
First are those in training (*śaikṣa*);
second are those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
From one who has seen the truths up to the stage of *anāgāmin*, these are called those in training.
The fruit of arhatship is called that of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
There are eighteen types of those in training (śaikṣa) and nine types of those beyond training; thus, in total, there are twenty-seven.
The eighteen scriptures for practitioners (*śaikṣa*) are listed out of order.
What are their names? The first is the practitioner of faith (*śraddhānusārin*).
Second is the practitioner of the Dharma (dharmānusārin);
third is the one liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta);
fourth is the one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
Fifth is the body-witness (kāyasākṣin).
Sixth is the one who goes from family to family (kulaṃkula).
Seventh is the one with only one seed remaining (ekabījī).
The eighth is the candidate for *srotāpanna*;
the ninth is the attainment of *srotāpanna*;
the tenth is the candidate for *sakṛdāgāmin*.
The eleventh attains the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin;
the twelfth is directed toward Anāgāmin;
the thirteenth attains the stage of Anāgāmin.
14. One who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state;
15. One who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth;
16. One who attains parinirvāṇa through practice.
Seventeenth, one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion;
eighteenth, the upstream-goer, who reaches Akaniṣṭha; these alone possess these specific names.
