According to the Abhidharma, those who practice through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and those who practice through dharma (dharmanusārin) reside within the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (darśanamārga);
the dull-witted are termed "those who practice through faith."

Regarding the names "Dharma-practitioner" (dharmānusārin) and "Faith-liberated" (śraddhāvimukta): according to the Abhidharma, these are situated within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), subsequent to the fruit of Srotāpanna.
The dull-witted are called "faith-liberated."
These four views— namely, those of gain, fame,
and philosophical speculation— comprehensively encompass all practitioners,
as they include all possible types.
The remaining fourteen persons are distinguished within this group.
From among those previously mentioned who are practitioners by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and practitioners by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), three persons are further differentiated:
first, the person who is a candidate for the stage of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*) following the sequential path.
One who enters the path of seeing within the fifteen moments of mind is called a candidate for the fruit of Srotāpanna (須陀洹向).
Furthermore, there is the candidate for the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin (斯陀含向), which is distinguished as follows:
one who transcends the [first] fruit and enters the path of seeing within the fifteen moments of mind is called a candidate for the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin.
Thirdly, the candidate for Anāgāmin (anāgāmipratipannaka) is separately distinguished.
One who transcends [the desire realm] and enters the path of seeing (darśanamārga), within the fifteen moments of mind, is called a candidate for Anāgāmin.

Among the previously mentioned types of persons—those liberated by faith (śraddhādhimukta) and those attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta)—thirteen distinct types of persons are separately distinguished.
The first reveals the fruit of srotāpanna;
the second reveals the candidate for the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin.
That is to say:
The person of gradual progression who is heading toward the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* but has not yet reached it,
and who previously practiced during the present life,
is the third type distinguished as one who belongs to the family-to-family (*kulaṃkula*).
This refers to those who follow the gradual path toward the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, who,
having severed the afflictions of the preliminary stage, are destined for direct rebirth.
The fourth [category] distinguishes the fruit of the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).
Within this, there is a further subdivision into two types:
the first is the one who attains the fruit of the once-returner by leaping over [the stages].
The two successive realizations of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* are collectively combined into a single fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*;
the fifth [stage] then separately establishes the candidate for the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
This refers to those who follow the gradual path and, while still directed toward the fruit of Anāgāmin,
are currently practicing in the present life prior to attaining that fruit.
The sixth category distinguishes a single type of person:
namely, the "successive person" (anupūrvaka) who, having directed themselves toward the stage of an Anāgāmin, abandons the afflictions and is reborn directly [in the Pure Abodes].
The seventh [category] distinguishes the fruit of anāgāmin;
within this, there are further two subdivisions.
The first is the one who attains the fruit of anāgāmin by leaping over.
The two successive realizations of the fruit of *anāgāmin* are now combined into a single fruit of *anāgāmin*,
while the eighth category is distinguished as those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*).
The ninth clarifies those who attain parinirvāṇa upon being born;
the tenth clarifies those who attain parinirvāṇa through exertion;
the eleventh clarifies those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion.
The twelve types of persons who attain parinirvāṇa by going upstream (ūrdhvasrotas) are distinguished as superior and inferior.
The superior ones attain parinirvāṇa within the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
The inferior ones are born within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and only then attain parinirvāṇa;
he mentions those who are superior.
Therefore it is said: "Reaching up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, those who are directed toward the field of merit and who exist within the realm of form—
possessing form and physical shape— are able to receive offerings and serve as a field of merit for the world."
This is a partial enumeration.
Among those who have attained the realization of their own body,
there are those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) subsequent to the fruit of anāgāmin.
These thirteen are all listed among those liberated through faith and those who have attained vision;
such is the case for those in training (śaikṣa). As for the nine types of those beyond training (aśaikṣa):
The sequence in the sutra is not arranged in order:
first, the one who contemplates the dharma;
second, the one who advances to the dharma.
Third, those of immovable nature;
fourth, those of a nature subject to regression;
fifth, those of a nature not subject to regression.
Sixth is the protection of the Dharma.
The Sūtra itself explains:
"To protect is to not regress."
Lack of protection leads to decline.
Seventh is abiding in the Dharma;
eighth is liberation through wisdom.
The ninth is "liberation through both.
Such is the scriptural text;
there is no other interpretation.
Among the nine [types], the first seven are distinguished according to their faculties (*indriya*),
while the latter two are defined in terms of their dharmas.
These seven types are analogous to the six types of arhats found in the Abhidharma.
The six arhats are those who fall back, those who dwell in thought, those who dwell in protection, those who progress upward, and those who are immovable.
In that *Āgama*, the immovable person is divided into two types;
therefore, there are seven.
Among the nine types of persons, those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) are the first type of person subject to falling away according to the Abhidharma;
among the nine, those of the nature of reflection (*cetayitadharman*) are the second type, the person of the nature of reflection;
and among the nine, those of the nature of guarding (*anurakṣaṇādharman*) are the third type, the person of the nature of guarding.
The "one who abides in the ninth" refers to the person of the fourth stage of abiding.
The "one who advances in the ninth" refers to the person of the fifth stage, the one destined for advancement.
The "one who is immovable in the ninth" and the "one who does not regress" refer to the person of the immovable type according to the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā).
In that Abhidharma, there are two kinds of immovability (*āneñjya*):
first, original immovability;
second, immovability attained through progress upon reaching the fruit.
Among the nine types, "immovable" (akopya) corresponds to what is called "immovable by reason of the cause" (hetu-akopya) in the Abhidharma;
"non-regressive" (anāvartin) corresponds to what is called "immovable by reason of having reached the fruit" (phala-akopya) in the Abhidharma.
The final two—liberation through wisdom (prajñā-vimukta) and liberation through both [wisdom and concentration] (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta)—are distinguished according to their respective dharmas.

Among the former seven types of persons, those who have not attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) are called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñā-vimukta). Those who have attained the absorption of cessation are called "doubly liberated" (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta).
These will be explained in detail later, following this section.

These twenty-seven [stages] include those who have not yet entered the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and the seven preliminary practices (*prayoga*); for such persons, there are thirty-four [stages].
In detail, they are immeasurable.
Such is the manner of their opening and closing.
The above constitutes the first section, the general classification of characteristics.
Next follows the second section, the detailed explanation according to specific categories.
The contemplations for settling the mind (pañca-vastu-pratipakṣa-bhāvanā) have been fully explained as in the preceding five chapters.
The general and specific applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) have been fully explained as previously detailed in the chapter on the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
The four stages, beginning with "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), have been extensively analyzed as previously presented in the section on the four types of wholesome states, beginning with "Heat."
Now, first, the candidate for the stage of Srotāpanna will be explained separately.
Within this, there are six analytical sections.
The first is the analysis according to the object (*ālambana*).
Second, the classification according to the number of categories;
third, the classification based on the unimpeded analytical knowledges and liberations;
fourth, the classification regarding cultivation.
Fifth, the determination of what is correct and incorrect; sixth, the distinction regarding the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*).
Regarding the statement "in terms of the object":
According to the Dharmaguptaka school, one realizes the truths simultaneously;
according to the Sarvāstivāda school, one realizes the truths sequentially.
Regarding the term "simultaneously," this is based on the tenets of that [Dharmaguptaka] school.
First, within the stages of Heat, Peak, and Patience prior to the Path of Seeing, one specifically contemplates the emptiness of each Truth separately until it becomes thoroughly matured.
Next, within the Supreme Mundane Dharma, one contemplates the Four Truths collectively, using their conventional designations as a provisional means of expression.
Subsequently, one enters the signless and comprehensively perceives that all dharmas of the Four Truths are empty;
this clarity increases moment by moment without interruption.
This principle is maintained within the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.
Regarding the terms "prior" and "subsequent": according to the Sarvāstivāda school, one attains the Path through distinct contemplations of the Four Noble Truths.
First, within the context of both general and specific mindfulness, the practitioner contemplates the Four Truths as a whole in terms of emptiness and non-self.
Yet, one has not yet attained clear understanding of the Four Noble Truths.
Within the four stages of the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, one takes the Four Noble Truths as distinct objects of focus as a preliminary practice;
from the stage of "Patience regarding Suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmakṣānti*) upward, one perceives them individually and clearly.
To view suffering as one thing and its origin as another, and to view cessation as one thing and the path as another,
is called "sequential viewing."
The various *Abhidharma* schools preserve this meaning.
A question is asked:
"Between these two, which one is correct?"
Both are Buddhas;
one should not rely exclusively on either.
However, there are differences between the two explanations based on the distinctions among individuals.
Those of dull faculties are unable to shatter appearances and perceive the emptiness of all phenomena;
they mostly rely on the sequential order of before and after to see the truths.
Those of sharp faculties are able to shatter the marks of existence and realize the emptiness of all phenomena.
Furthermore, they rely on the same time period.
Moreover, the two schools establish their respective afflictions differently;
according to the Dharmaguptaka school, [ignorance] is taken as the root of affliction.
Although one has not yet finished separately perceiving the truths and abandoning grasping,
it is only when one perceives emptiness as a whole that grasping and its afflictions are exhausted.
For this reason, in contemplating the truths, one first contemplates them individually and subsequently as a whole.
According to the Sarvāstivāda, delusion is the root of affliction;
although the characteristic of darkness is not yet dispelled through general contemplation of the truths,
it is only exhausted through specific contemplation that renders the characteristic of darkness clear.
Thus, according to that school, first the general and then the specific [classification] concludes this section.
Next, the meaning of the number of categories will be explained.
According to the Abhidharma, within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are only fifteen moments of mind.
The fruit of Srotāpanna comprises sixteen moments of mind;
these sixteen consist of eight patiences (kṣānti) and eight knowledges (jñāna).
Regarding the contemplation of suffering in the desire realm, there is first patience and subsequently knowledge.
There are two moments of mind.
Regarding the observation of suffering in the higher realms, there are likewise two moments of mind: the initial patience and the subsequent knowledge.
The same applies to the remaining truths.
If one relies on the *Tattvasiddhi*, there are immeasurable minds within the stage of the path of seeing;
thus, that text states:
One cuts off all afflictions by means of immeasurable minds (*apramāṇacitta*).
It is neither eight nor nine.
Regarding "not eight," this refers to the teaching that within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), there is a continuity of immeasurable minds that sever the delusions.
Refuting the Abhidharma’s fixed doctrine of eight patiences,
he states that they are not nine, asserting instead that within the path of cultivation there are immeasurable minds.
Refuting the Abhidharma’s fixed position that there are nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) for each stage (*bhūmi*), he argues against this certainty.
For what reason does the Abhidharma definitively teach eight patiences?
In that school, the contemplation of existence (bhava) takes the characteristics of existence as its specific and restricted object.
Because it is easy to see and clear.
Why does the *Tattvasiddhi* state that the immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*) of that school contemplate emptiness?
Because emptiness has no boundaries and is difficult to perceive. Thus ends this section on the two gates.
Next, regarding the analysis of the unhindered knowledges (pratisaṃvid) and liberations (vimokṣa):
according to the Abhidharma, within the stage of the path of seeing (darśanamārga), one abandons the afflictions of the views by means of both the unhindered knowledge and the liberation paths.
The eight patiences constitute non-obstruction;
the seven knowledges constitute liberation.
There should thus be eight knowledges.
The last one is judged to be the fruit of Srotāpanna;
therefore, only seven are mentioned.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, within the state of non-characteristics, there is only unimpeded [knowledge] without liberation.
Why is this so? According to that school’s doctrine, both the unhindered [knowledges] and liberation are identical to the contemplation of emptiness;
it is within this state that further progress is described as being "unhindered."
The wisdom that accords with the ancient [teachings] is judged to be liberation;
the liberation that accords with the ancient [teachings] is judged to belong to the stage of Srotāpanna.
Therefore, there is nothing intermediate, only the pure absence of hindrance. This concludes the three gates.
Next, the fourth section distinguishes [the practice] according to cultivation.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the extent of cultivation by way of the objects of focus.
Second, regarding the extent of cultivation, it is clarified by way of the mind engaged in practice.
As for "by way of the object," it is as explained in the Abhidharma:
within those fifteen moments of mind of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), one realizes a single truth (*satya*).
In the future, one further clarifies the single truth (*satya*).
In the present observation (*abhisamaya*), one further clarifies the four modes (*ākāra*) subordinate to the single truth through the single mode.
This is because all that is observed is clearly understood.
Because the four aspects of each of the truths are closely related, they all become increasingly clear.
A question is asked:
Within the four types of present-forbearance (*kṣānti*), when one truth is presently realized, does that which is future increase in clarity by being applied to the other four truths?
In the clear realization (*abhisamaya*), a single category [of knowledge] in the future is augmented by sixteen [moments] as it becomes increasingly luminous;
this principle also applies up to the sixteenth moment, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
Why, then, is it not the same in the fifteen moments of this path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)?
In the future, one will only further clarify a single truth;
one will only further clarify the four aspects of that same truth.
Thus it is explained.
The four present paths and the subsequent path of inference constitute the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*).
Because the mental resolve is expansive, one cultivates much expansiveness.
These fifteen moments of mind constitute the path of rapid progress (*kṣipra-mārga*).
Because their aspirations are lofty yet narrow, their cultivation is likewise narrow and meager. This has been explained in terms of the objects [of meditation].
Next, the extent of cultivation will be clarified in terms of the mental states of practice.
Cultivation is of two kinds:
first, cultivation through practice,
which arises manifestly in relation to its objects.
Second is cultivation by acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*). This refers to bringing that which is being cultivated under one's own mastery.

For instance, when practicing according to the cultivation of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), one cultivates and acquires only the mind of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering.
Up until the moment of the subsequent-knowledge-forbearance (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) of the final path, one can only cultivate the mind of that subsequent-knowledge-forbearance.
This is according to the simultaneous acquisition of what is cultivated;
alternatively, it may be acquired later than what preceded it.
It is not that the former acquires the latter,
because the latter does not acquire the former; thus,
at the initial moment of the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*, there are fifteen acquisitions of acquisitions (*prāpti-prāpti*).
Up until the final moment of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), there is only the acquisition of a single acquisition (*prāpti*).
What is its characteristic?
At the time when the dharma-patience regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmakṣānti*) arises, [this occurs].
There is a dharma that is neither form nor mind which arises simultaneously with patience (*kṣānti*). When one attains the present *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*,
one also attains its homogeneous types (*sabhāgajāti*) existing in the future, causing them to come under one's own possession and achieve [the state of] "one who has lost" (*ekahīna*).
Question: That patience is acquired through attainment and remains with oneself without being lost;
by what means is that attainment acquired so that it remains with oneself without being lost?
The commentary says:
That [attainment] is not lost because it is further obtained by means of a minor attainment (*parīttalābha*).
By what is this minor attainment obtained?
Furthermore, it is due to the acquisition of the great [attainment] that [the dharma] is not lost;
this is like two births mutually producing one another.
Although there are two acquisitions, because they are now combined as a whole, they are spoken of as a single acquisition.
The others are also like this.
Question: It was previously stated that the latter is obtained after the former, and the former is not obtained after the latter.
Now, why is it said that the category of those who have attained [the path] exists in the future?
The explanation states: as for the previous statement that "those who have not yet attained it" are excluded, [it refers to this].
When one attains the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), one does not fail to attain the subsequent dharma-knowledges (*dharmajñāna*) regarding suffering and so forth;
it is not that one fails to attain the future categories belonging to the present arising [state].
These future categories, though not yet arisen in relation to the present, are still termed "already arisen."
Because it is of a similar type to what has already arisen, at the time of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), two acquisitions (*prāpti*) arise simultaneously:
one is the acquisition of the knowledge of suffering, and the other is the acquisition of the preceding mind of the dharma-forbearance of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).
In this manner they gradually increase,
until finally, at the time of the patience that precedes the path (*mārgānvaya-kṣānti*),
there are fifteen acquisitions (*prāpti*) that arise simultaneously with it.
First is the attainment of the path;
the remaining fourteen attainments acquire the preceding fourteen.
Question: [What is this?]
Subsequently attained [wisdom] only attains the essential nature of the dharmas previously attained;
it also attains the prior attainment itself,
though the interpretation of this meaning is not fixed.
Explaining it according to a single principle:
one only obtains the preceding dharma; the preceding acquisition (*prāpti*) that follows that dharma also becomes non-forfeited (*avipraṇāśa*).
Explain this by means of a single principle:
it universally obtains what was previously obtained.
If that were so, there would be the fault of infinite regress through mutual dependence.
The commentary’s own explanation states:
"What fault is there in infinite regress?
The meaning of cultivation is thus. This concludes the four gates.
Next, to determine what is right and wrong,
he asked: "In the context of what you have seen, what do you take to be the Way?"
There are four distinct levels of meaning.
Regarding the first meaning: wisdom is the essence of the Path; all else is not.
Because without wisdom one cannot endure the knowledge of dharmas.
According to the second meaning, wisdom, all mental states and their concomitants, as well as the precepts of the Path, together constitute the Right Path.

Because the Eightfold Noble Path takes this as its essence, the four characteristics (lakṣaṇas) associated with the attainment of the various paths are not designated as the "Noble Path" according to their respective meanings.
Regarding the third meaning: mental factors, ethical discipline, and the four characteristics arise simultaneously and together; they are thus co-existent causes (sahabhū-hetu).
When mutual support is based on the sense of righteousness and intimacy, it is generally described as a path (*mārga*).
However, when various attainments (*prāpti*) arise in anticipation of that [path] and involve the arising of precepts at different times, they are not considered co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*),
because their mutual support is based on a loose sense of righteousness and is therefore not described as a path.
Regarding the fourth meaning: the mental factors, the precepts, the various acquisitions (prāpti), and the four characteristics (lakṣaṇa) all possess the sense of mutually supporting one another;
collectively, these are explained as the Path. It is asked:
If one relies on the first three meanings, then various acquisitions (*prāpti*) would also not be the path, nor would they be the fruit.
Furthermore, "fruit" carries the sense of being attained and realized;
various acquisitions accord with the fruit.
Therefore, it is called a "fruit" (*phala*).
Since the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) constitutes the stage of application (*prayoga*), why does the treatise state that "attainment" (*prāpti*) is the fruit?
The commentary states:
In the treatise, it is taught that "attainment" (*prāpti*) constitutes a fruit;
this accords with the latter of the two meanings.
Because it does not turn toward [the supramundane], it is not called the Path.
The attainment of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*) is also explained in the same way as to why it is not called "Supreme" (*agra*). Question:
If one were to claim that it is called the "Path" based on the latter of these two meanings,
the treatise states:
"One who has attained that Worldly Supreme Dharma (laukikāgra-dharma) is not said to have attained the 'First'."
Now, why is it said that the attainment of the Path is also called the Path?
The explanation is as follows:
the treatise speaks of "attainment" as being both the supreme attainment and the non-supreme attainment.
This is the same as the threefold meaning of non-path mentioned previously.
Furthermore, the stage of the World’s Supreme Dharma (laukikāgra-dharma) is brief, lasting for only a single moment;
the acquisitions (prāpti) preceding and following it span many moments and are therefore not concordant with that [momentary state].
Because that attainment is not called "supreme," and because the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is broad and long, consisting of many moments,
it is designated as the "path" (*mārga*) due to its conformity with those [attainments].
This concludes the five gates as explained above.
Next, we shall provide an analysis based on the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*).
A question is asked:
Seeing that the central path is steep and swift, one attains the transformation of the faculties; it is not otherwise.
Thus it is said.
It is not so. This is because there are no multiple conditions for each individual factor. One asks:
If one says that [the fruit] is definitely not attained,

it contradicts the Abhidharma, which declares in its treatises that both the person of faith (śraddhānusārin) and the person who follows the Dharma (dharmānusārin) abide together in the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
Faithful practice is the cause for the practice of that Dharma;
why, then, would it not proceed?
Furthermore, he explains again:
While there is a sense in which an inferior aspiration may serve as a cause for a superior principle,
in reality it does not transform.
If one relies on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, since both are the same contemplation of emptiness, it is truly difficult to transform the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*).

If one relies on the *Abhidharma*, it is possible for there to be the sense of "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) regarding the contemplation of the truths through their distinctions. What is the meaning of this?
Generally, one who transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) contemplates many objects and is likewise able to transform their faculties.
Through forceful application toward the object, one can also transform the faculties by means of clear and pure mental observation.
Regarding the Dharma of the Four Truths, they are initially easy to understand but become difficult to comprehend as one progresses.
When a practitioner trains in the contemplation of the truths within the four types of patience (*kṣānti*) of the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), there are five distinct varieties.
There is a type of person who has not yet discerned the Four Noble Truths;
lacking the power of effort regarding suffering,
such a person enters the path of vision solely as one who practices through faith.
As for the second person, among the four levels of patience regarding the present (*caturvidhābhisamaya-kṣānti*), they have not yet cultivated mature observation regarding the first three truths;
they observe with the path as their object through strenuous effort.
When such a person enters the stage of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), their vision of the first three truths is not yet extremely clear.
This is called "practice through faith" (*śraddhānusārin*).
Later, when the Truth of the Path is clearly perceived and understood, it is transformed into "practice through the Dharma" (*dharmānusārin*).
As for the third person, among the four types of patience regarding the present, they have not yet been able to investigate the first two Truths.
Regarding cessation and the path, they apply themselves with difficulty and exert effort in contemplation;
such a person, upon entering the vision [of the truths], does not possess extreme clarity in their vision of suffering and its origin,
and is thus called a "follower by faith" (śraddhānusārin).
Regarding cessation and the path, one attains clear illumination and turns toward the practice of the Dharma;
as for the fourth person, among the four types of present patience (*kṣānti*), they have not yet been able to investigate the first truth, the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Regarding the latter three truths, he finds them difficult to apply and must exert effort to observe them.
When such a person enters the path of seeing, their insight into the first truth, suffering (*duḥkha*), is not yet extremely clear;
they are thus judged to be a follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*).
Regarding the latter three truths, one clearly perceives and understands them, thereby transforming this into the practice of the Dharma.
As for the fifth person, during the four stages of patience toward the manifest, they apply diligent effort toward all four noble truths.

When such a person enters the vision of the Four Noble Truths and perceives them with complete clarity, they enter the Path of Seeing the Truths (darśanamārga) solely by way of Dharma-practice (dharmānusārin).
Among the five types of persons, the first and the last are not said to undergo a transformation of their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra).
The middle three names refer to the "turnings.
This has been a brief explanation of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala-pratipannaka*).
Next, the fruit of stream-entry itself will be explained in detail.
The candidate for the stage of Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka) is also included within the category of stream-enterers (srotāpanna) when discussed collectively as a single group.
Within this, there are six sections of analysis:
first, the determination of its essential nature.
Second, explaining the attainment and relinquishment;
third, explaining the number of fetters severed by a srotāpanna;
fourth, explaining the number of bodies received by a srotāpanna.
Fifth, the *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family). Sixth, the distinction between those of dull and sharp faculties.
Regarding the essential nature of concentration (*samādhi*), its substance is the noble virtue of the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
The noble virtues differ, and in general, there are three [aspects].
The first is the essence of the fruit (*phala-bhāva*).

According to the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā), when analyzing the cultivation of practice, only the sixteenth moment of mind—the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*)—is its essence as the fruit.

According to the *Vibhāṣā*, the sixteen noble minds of the vision of the truths (*darśanamārga*), which are subsumed under the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), all constitute the essence of the fruit.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, however, it is the subsequent emptiness-contemplation (*śūnyatā-bhāvanā*) that accords with the ancient tradition which constitutes the essence of the fruit.
Second, the path of equal vision in training (*śaikṣa-samadarśana-mārga*):

after attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), one dwells in contemplation of the untainted (*anāsrava*) while repeatedly taking the principles of the truths as objects, yet does not further advance.
Third, the path of the superior fruit (*viśeṣa-phala-mārga*).
After attaining the fruit of srotāpanna, one further gives rise to superior resolve (*adhimokṣa*) to advance and sever the fetters of desire,
whether one, two, or even up to six categories. Regarding this practice,
upon which truth (*satya*) does it take its object as one advances to sever the afflictions?
Among the Four Noble Truths, one proceeds by taking a single truth as the object.
A question is asked:
Why, previously, when severing the delusions of views, did one take all four truths as objects?
This abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) relies solely upon a single truth (satya).
The commentary explains:
previously, one abandoned the afflictions that are delusions regarding the truths.
Since one is universally deluded regarding all four truths,
it is necessary to contemplate them collectively;
this abandonment of greed, hatred, and delusion directed toward objective conditions does not occur through abandoning a general delusion.
Therefore, regarding the four truths, after one has attained the fruit that can sever [defilements] by taking a single aspect as an object,
a question is asked:
"Since this practice takes the principle of the truths as its object..."
How can one sever the afflictions that take objects as their conditions?
If one relies on the Abhidharma to contemplate the subtle while abandoning the coarse,
then one is able to sever them.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, all afflictions arise from grasping at intrinsic nature;
therefore, contemplating emptiness to destroy this nature is what can sever them.
Question: Is the principle of truth observed through this practice deeper than that which previously served to abandon the afflictions of the path of cultivation,
or is it the same as the former in its ability to abandon the afflictions of the path of cultivation?
If it were to become even deeper, what characteristic would there be?
If it were not deep, how could it differ from cessation?
This is one interpretation.
Because this practice contemplates the principle more profoundly, it is able to differ from [ordinary] abandonment.
However, these profound characteristics are difficult to distinguish by their respective stages;
they can only be personally realized by the Sages and cannot be differentiated through words.
This is like the afflictions of the nine grades within each stage (*bhūmi*), which are difficult to distinguish individually;
it is also like the nine grades of innate wholesome roots (*upapattilābhika-kuśalamūla*) within each stage, which are difficult to differentiate.
Although they cannot be distinguished, there is nonetheless a gradation of levels.
This is also like that. Furthermore,
it is explained that this practice of contemplation shares the same principle as the former, yet it is also capable of effecting abandonment through differentiation.
Why is this so? Although the principle is the same as before, one repeatedly contemplates the mind-ground and repeatedly contemplates the clarity of the mind.
Therefore, they can differ in their abandonment [of afflictions].
This is like a certain medicine: a small dose reduces illness, while a large dose can eliminate it entirely.
It is not that because many illnesses are cured there are correspondingly many different medicines;
it is just as a single meal may slightly alleviate hunger,
yet eating much will completely eliminate it.
It is not that many [people] are exhausted by hunger so that they must eat different things;
this case is likewise.
Although the holy virtues of a Srotāpanna are immeasurable, they are essentially comprised of only these three.
The analysis of the essence [of the stages] concludes with this section.
Next, we shall discuss attainment and relinquishment based on their sequence;
first, we will treat the meaning of relinquishment.
Question: When a *srotāpanna* attains the fruit, does he abandon his previous stage of "heading toward" (*pratipannaka*), or does he not?
According to the Abhidharma, at the moment of realizing the fruit, one definitely abandons the previous stage of heading toward it.
Equanimity is of two kinds.
First, regarding its cultivation through practice:
non-practice is called equanimity.
Because the preceding fifteen moments of mind do not manifest at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
Second, regarding cultivation by acquisition (*pratilambhabhāvanā*): the attainment of abandonment is termed "relinquishment" (*tyāga*).
Because the fruit arises once the cause has been severed.
Even according to the *Tattvasiddhi*, it is abandoned;
for in reality, as the causal mind passes away through its subtle divisions, the resultant mind manifests.
This is termed "equanimity" (upekṣā).
In the theory of continuity, the cause reaching its fulfillment constitutes the fruit;
it does not involve the relinquishing of what was previously attained.
This is called "non-abandonment. Question:
Does the Srotāpanna cultivate the path of further progress?
When one is about to become a Sakṛdāgāmin, does one abandon the previous fruit?
The explanation says:
one does not abandon it.
Why is this so? Because their resolve to realize the fruit is profound, they do not abandon it.
Furthermore, although a Srotāpanna may initiate superior practices, they cease of their own accord, relying solely upon their previous fruit.
It is for this reason that one does not abandon it.
Next, the meaning of attainment will be discussed. Question:
When a Srotāpanna realizes the first fruit,
does he attain the preceding stage of approach as being subsumed within the subsequent fruit,
or does he not so attain it?
This is as explained previously.
According to the Abhidharma, cultivation is of two kinds:
the first is cultivation by practice (āsevana-bhāvanā).
The second is cultivation by acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*).
If based on cultivation by practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*), within the fruit there is only the mind of subsequent inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and not the preceding fifteen [moments].
If based on cultivation by acquisition, one acquires the preceding [moments] of the path of approach, which together constitute the subsequent fruit.
What is the meaning of this?
Upon realizing the first fruit (*phala*), one abandons the fifteen distinct acquisitions of the preceding path of approach (*prayoga-mārga*) and attains,
as a single whole, the innate path and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Furthermore, one obtains the fifteen untainted [factors] within the stage of "heading toward" (pratipannaka), which are combined to constitute the state of Srotāpanna.
A question is asked:
Should the merits obtained while directly heading toward [the fruit] be combined with those of the subsequent fruit?
Furthermore, can the attainment that is acquired within the intermediate state serve as a subsequent fruit?
The interpretation of this principle is not fixed;
it shall be explained according to one sense.
Only the attained untainted merits (anāsrava-guṇa) are combined to constitute the subsequent fruit;
that which is capable of attaining [them] is not so included. Why is this so?
The essence of the dharma that is attained possesses the meaning of being both distinct and pervasive;
therefore, it is attained again.
The "attainment" that is the agent of attainment is not the true essence of the dharma.
Since these two are mutually exclusive and distinct,
there is no principle by which they could be established as mutually inclusive; therefore, this is untenable.
Furthermore, among the acquired mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), the mind-factor (*citta-dharma*) is primary.
When a mental factor arises, it necessarily possesses a category that is established in the future;
for there exists in the future the principle that it may arise.
Later, one obtains them again and combines them to form a fruit.
These are not mental factors (citta-dharma),
as there is no sense of broad pervasiveness existing in the future.
Therefore, they cannot subsequently combine to produce their fruit.
Because there is this distinction,
it is said in the treatise:
Having abandoned the previous [attainment], one may further give rise to the attainment of the fruit;
thus, the attainment of the previous dharma is combined to constitute the fruit.
Furthermore, this shall be explained again.
It is logically unobjectionable that one simultaneously attains the preceding dharma and the preceding acquisition,
combining them to constitute the subsequent fruit.
Therefore, the treatise asks:
If there were attainment, there would be the fault of infinite regress.
The treatise itself explains:
"What is the harm in infinite regress?"
Question: If it is the case that when a fruit arises, one simultaneously attains the previous attainments,
what then is meant by "severing" and what is meant by "abandoning"?
Although one may obtain it, it is not of that same category;
therefore, it is called "abandonment.
Such is the Abhidharma.
If, according to the *Tattvasiddhi*, one establishes only the cultivation of practice (*caryā-bhāvanā*) and not the cultivation of attainment (*prāpti-bhāvanā*),
then for this reason it is not stated that the attainment [of the fruit] is combined with the preceding stage of application (*prayoga*) to constitute the subsequent fruit. Question:
When a *srotāpanna* arises from the superior practice and turns toward the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*,
does one who has attained the former fruit become a candidate for the latter?
The commentary says:
Since the prior fruit is not relinquished when one arises later facing [a different direction], there is no distinct acquisition (*prāpti*).
Such is the relinquishment of acquisitions; these two sections are hereby concluded.
Next, the treatise discusses the number of fetters (*saṃyojana*) severed by the *srotāpanna*.
The Sūtra states:
"The *srotāpanna* severs only three fetters."
These are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*). It is asked:
The Sūtra says:
The afflictions severed by a srotāpanna are like a pond forty li in length and breadth;
those that remain are like a single drop.
Why, then, do you say that he has severed only the three fetters?
The commentary states:
Although that which is abandoned by the *srotāpanna* is in fact vast,
these three [fetters] are specifically mentioned for four reasons.
First, these three are the root of all afflictions; by mentioning them, the others are subsumed.
Therefore, only these three are specifically taught.
What is the root of the afflictions?
The ten fetters that delude one regarding the truths are all severed by the *srotāpanna*.
Among these ten fetters, the five views and doubt obstruct only the vision of the truths;
since the *srotāpanna* has severed them completely, they are specifically designated as "severed."
Greed, hatred, delusion, and pride generally obstruct both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
Those that obstruct the path of seeing are completely severed by the stage of Srotāpanna;
those that obstruct the path of cultivation have not yet been eliminated by the Srotāpanna.
Because they have not been completely severed, they are not designated by the term "severed.
Among those six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that are to be severed, three are primary (mūla) and three are secondary (anuvartin).
The view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is the primary one.
Extreme views follow from it;
the clinging to precepts and observances is the root;
the clinging to views follows from it.
Doubt is fundamentally accompanied by wrong view;
since the sutra speaks of the root, it mentions only three, for even when these have not yet been abandoned, they continue to follow along.
These two are mentioned specifically because they are particularly grave.
As explained in the commentary on *Nirvāṇa*:
for example, when a worldly king comes or goes,
although there are many ministers and attendants, because the king is preeminent, people speak of him specifically.
These three are mentioned specifically because they are so weighty.
How are they weighty?
That sutra explains:
Because it is constantly aroused by all sentient beings,
and because it is difficult to awaken from;
it is like a chronic illness that constantly flares up, constituting a grave malady.
Furthermore, that which is difficult to recognize and know is called a "grave illness.
These three are such;
because sentient beings constantly give rise to them without realizing they are faults, they are said to be grave.
Third, these three are specifically mentioned because they can act as great enemies to all three trainings—of ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
How do they act as enemies?
In accordance with their characteristics, they are coarse adversaries that obstruct ethical discipline.
Doubt is called the enemy of ethical discipline;
the hindrance of doubt obstructs meditative concentration and is thus called the enemy of concentration.
The view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) obstructs wisdom and is thus called the enemy of wisdom; however,

He says: The view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) can act as an enemy to the precepts;
it conceives of the soul as permanent, indifferent to suffering and pleasure, and does not fear the fruits of karma.
Indulging the passions to commit transgressions obstructs the cultivation of pure precepts; thus, it is the enemy of the precepts.
Attachment to precepts is the enemy of meditative concentration.
Adherence to mere rules and rituals as the path obstructs the cultivation of superior tranquility and is therefore the enemy of concentration;
doubt is the enemy of wisdom,
for it causes hesitation regarding objects and prevents decisive understanding.
Because it obstructs right knowledge, it is the enemy of wisdom.
The three [types of ignorance] are taught according to the needs of those to be converted,
as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
There may be sentient beings who, upon hearing it said that a *srotāpanna* severs immeasurable fetters, lose heart and do not seek [the goal];
therefore, only three [fetters] are mentioned.
Such is what is severed. This concludes the section on these three gates.
